newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican state governor rejects drugs charges.
newsitem.headline: Mexican state governor rejects drugs charges.

text.p: A Mexican state governor accused in a New York Times article of complicity with drug traffickers rejected the charges on Sunday as a farrago of lies aimed at undermining Mexico's anti-narcotics fight.

The newspaper, citing U.S. officials and intelligence sources, said the governor of the border state of Sonora, Manlio Fabio Beltrones, had helped create a haven for smugglers who ship vast quantities of drugs into the United States but that he enjoyed political immunity.
The governor of Morelos state, Jorge Carrillo Olea, was also on a U.S. blacklist because of reported links with major drug dealers, the paper said.

"I categorically reject these statements," Beltrones said in a statement released Sunday. "They look like a clumsy retailing of lies...presenting a capricious list of isolated assumptions that someone has tried to link with perverse or malicious imagination to produce a false tale."

Beltrones took part in meetings in which leading traffickers paid high-level politicians, including Raul Salinas, the brother of Mexico's former president, with suitcases full of cash for protecting their operations, the officials told the paper.

The evidence against Beltrones, whose state borders Arizona, was so strong that the United States named him in a confidential report to the transition team of President Ernesto Zedillo listing Mexican officials suspected of corruption, the New York Times said.
Carrillo could not be reached for comment on Sunday but has denied any link to drug-traffickers.

Beltrones said the charges appeared to be part of campaign to embarrass Mexico ahead of a decision to be taken by the Clinton administration within a week on whether to certify that Mexico is cooperating with anti-drug efforts.
"I see a counter-campaign that seeks to prejudice institutions and public officials who collaborate to make the binational fight against organised crime effective," he said.
The Times said officials on both sides of the border were frustrated by the tacit immunity enjoyed by the governors.

President Ernesto Zedillo, in an interview broadcast Sunday but recorded before the New York Times story appeared, pledged to tell Mexicans the truth when drug-corruption in government was discovered.

"It is a grave problem which we are facing...by telling the truth," Zedillo said. "At no time has it passed through my mind that we should cover up this situation simply to avoid the national embarrassment and shame that this has caused."

He was referring to the sudden arrest of its top drug warrior last week on charges he took money from the country's most powerful cocaine lord, Amado Carrillo Fuentes -- the same trafficker linked to Beltrones by the New York Times.
The dismissal of the top drug fighter, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, embarrassed both the U.S. and the Mexican governments.

One of Gutierrez's sons, in an interview in Reforma newspaper published on Sunday, denied that his father was involved in corruption and said unnamed military officers had telephoned the family to say his arrest was "treason, ...a lie."

Despite recent disclosures of corruption, senior U.S. officials told the New York Times that Clinton plans to "certify" Mexico, reflecting a belief that Mexico's leadership is doing all it can against staggering odds.

Law enforcement officials feel the Clinton administration considers the narcotics war less important than fostering commerce with Mexico, the United States' third largest trade partner, the Times said.
